cases.title: REQ-1-1-1: registration entry accepts valid account and redirects to sign-in without exposing password
cases.basis: Atomic description + inherited role, scope, state and entry contracts; source review only
cases.requirement_quote:
The registration page is the form opened by the unique link named “Create an account” from the sign-in page. The form contains exactly one textbox labeled “Username”, one textbox labeled “Email”, one password input labeled “Password”, one password input labeled “Confirm password”, one initially unchecked checkbox named “Agree to the terms”, and one enabled button named “Create account”. The username and email identify the account, while passwords must not be echoed on the page. This product directly marks the email of a successfully registered account as verified and does not provide a subsequent email-verification page. The visitor enters a unique username, email, password, and matching confirmation, checks “Agree to the terms”, and activates “Create account”. The username must consist of 1 to 39 lowercase ASCII letters, digits, or single hyphens (`-`) and must not begin or end with a hyphen; after trimming leading and trailing whitespace, the email must contain exactly one `@`, be no longer than 254 characters, and have at least one dot and non-empty domain labels after the `@`; the password must contain 12 to 128 characters, include at least one uppercase letter, one lowercase letter, one digit, and one non-alphanumeric special character, and contain no whitespace characters. The system stores a sign-in-capable account together with its verified-email status and enters the sign-in page; if the username or email conflicts, any field is missing, the email format is invalid, the terms are not accepted, the password is noncompliant, or the confirmation does not match, the system retains the username and email input, displays an itemized message beside the corresponding field, and does not create an account. The corresponding visible field message contains “Username already exists”, “Username format is invalid”, “Email format is invalid”, “Password requirements are not satisfied”, or “Agree to terms is required”, as applicable. Visitors can use this capability on the account-access page. The system validates input rules, displays field errors, and prevents duplicate accounts; on success, it directly creates an available account. Submitting several invalid fields together must show the username, email, password, and missing-terms messages together, rather than revealing only one error per submission; the submit button remains actionable so these messages can be read. For example, a username beginning with a hyphen, email “not-an-email”, password “short”, confirmation “different”, and unchecked terms produce these field errors and preserve the attempted username. A duplicate username paired with a different unused email displays “Username already exists” and retains both attempted values. A successful registration accepts a unique username, its email, and password; the sign-in form is immediately available, accepts that email, and the resulting signed-in username remains visible after reload.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-sign-up.png)

The form contains exactly one textbox labeled “Username”, one textbox labeled “Email”, one password input labeled “Password”, one password input labeled “Confirm password”, one initially unchecked checkbox named “Agree to the terms”, and one enabled button named “Create account”. The username and email identify the account, while passwords must not be echoed on the page. This product directly marks the email of a successfully registered account as verified and does not provide a subsequent email-verification page. The visitor enters a unique username, email, password, and matching confirmation, checks “Agree to the terms”, and activates “Create account”. The username must consist of 1 to 39 lowercase ASCII letters, digits, or single hyphens (`-`) and must not begin or end with a hyphen; after trimming leading and trailing whitespace, the email must contain exactly one `@`, be no longer than 254 characters, and have at least one dot and non-empty domain labels after the `@`; the password must contain 12 to 128 characters, include at least one uppercase letter, one lowercase letter, one digit, and one non-alphanumeric special character, and contain no whitespace characters. The system stores a sign-in-capable account together with its verified-email status and enters the sign-in page; if the username or email conflicts, any field is missing, the email format is invalid, the terms are not accepted, the password is noncompliant, or the confirmation does not match, the system retains the username and email input, displays an itemized message beside the corresponding field, and does not create an account. The corresponding visible field message contains “Username already exists”, “Username format is invalid”, “Email format is invalid”, “Password requirements are not satisfied”, or “Agree to terms is required”, as applicable. Visitors can use this capability on the account-access page. The system validates input rules, displays field errors, and prevents duplicate accounts; on success, it directly creates an available account. Submitting several invalid fields together must show the username, email, password, and missing-terms messages together, rather than revealing only one error per submission; the submit button remains actionable so these messages can be read. For example, a username beginning with a hyphen, email “not-an-email”, password “short”, confirmation “different”, and unchecked terms produce these field errors and preserve the attempted username. A duplicate username paired with a different unused email displays “Username already exists” and retains both attempted values. A successful registration accepts a unique username, its email, and password; the sign-in form is immediately available, accepts that email, and the resulting signed-in username remains visible after reload.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-sign-up.png)

The system stores a sign-in-capable account together with its verified-email status and enters the sign-in page; if the username or email conflicts, any field is missing, the email format is invalid, the terms are not accepted, the password is noncompliant, or the confirmation does not match, the system retains the username and email input, displays an itemized message beside the corresponding field, and does not create an account. The corresponding visible field message contains “Username already exists”, “Username format is invalid”, “Email format is invalid”, “Password requirements are not satisfied”, or “Agree to terms is required”, as applicable. requirement_quotes.REQ-1-1-2:
This feature builds on the persisted objects. The sign-in page is the form on the account-access page containing “Username or email”, “Password”, and “Sign in”. A “session” is the current-browser login record saved after successful account authentication, represented in the frontend by the upper-right account menu and access to protected pages. The visitor enters a username or email and a password and submits the form. The system looks up the account and validates its credentials and availability status; if authentication fails due to an unknown username/email, incorrect password, or unavailable account, the system displays exactly the same generic failure message “Invalid credentials”, does not disclose whether the account exists or which credential was wrong, and does not create a session. After successful authentication, the system stores a session with a unique session identifier, account identifier, and active status, then redirects to the workspace accessible to that user; the session remains valid after refreshing or reopening the workspace, and subsequent protected organization, repository, and work-item requests must use this session to determine the current user.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-sign-in.png)

cases.title: REQ-1-3: password change uses current account and old password no longer signs in
cases.basis: Atomic description + inherited role, scope, state and entry contracts; source review only
cases.requirement_quote:
This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes. The security form has uniquely labeled password inputs “Current password”, “New password”, and “Confirm password”, and a button “Update password”; submitting an empty current-password field must display the visible application message “Current password is required”. A failure with an incorrect current password and confirmation “does-not-match” must display the corresponding current-password or confirmation error and leave the old credentials usable. Each password-change scenario starts with its own verified account in the stated credential state and a different compliant candidate password. “Password and authentication” is the security page in account Settings used to change the current account credentials; the change affects only the current account's password record and does not alter any other accounts or resources outside the session. The user must provide the current password, a new password compliant with the REQ-1 password rules, and a character-for-character identical confirmation password; all three fields are required. The system validates the change, prevents unauthorized updates, and applies the new password to subsequent sign-in attempts. If the current password is incorrect, the new password is noncompliant, the confirmation does not match, or any field is missing, the system displays the reason in the corresponding field and does not modify the credentials; the applicable visible message is “Current password is incorrect”, “Password confirmation does not match”, or “Current password is required”. The old password remains valid and the new password must not work for sign-in. After a successful update, the page displays “Password updated”, the new password is immediately used for subsequent password-based sign-ins, and the old password must no longer work for new sign-ins.

Seed password-change values are `New-password-456!` for the successful update and
`Required-password-789!` for the missing-current-password scenario.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-password-settings.png)

cases.title: REQ-2-1-1: organization live repository filter exposes public result and hides private result
cases.basis: Atomic description + inherited role, scope, state and entry contracts; source review only
cases.requirement_quote:
The organization page presents “Repositories” as a navigation link, visually usable as a tab, and a textbox labeled “Find a repository”. Filtering updates the visible results as the user types, without a separate submit action. Each result has a link named exactly with the repository name, and opens a heading displaying “organization name/repository name”. Returning with browser Back keeps the public result available; filtering by the exact private repository name never exposes its link to a visitor. The seed organization has a public repository and a distinct private repository inaccessible to visitors. From the organization page, the user clicks the “Repositories” link, can enter a repository name in the filter box, select a public/private filter, and click a repository name in the list to open its overview. The system displays only the names, descriptions, visibility, and update times of repositories visible to the current user; clicking a result opens that repository's overview. Visitors can view public repositories on a public organization overview page; signed-in accounts can see only repositories for which they have read permission on the Repositories tab of the organization overview. The list reads repository name, description, visibility, and update time and provides no write operations; private repositories must first be validated under the already defined repository-access rules.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-organization-repositories.png)

cases.title: REQ-3-1: global search opens public identity and excludes private repository
cases.basis: Atomic description + inherited role, scope, state and entry contracts; source review only
cases.requirement_quote:
The top global search control has searchbox role and accessible name “Search”; entering a repository name and pressing Enter displays repository results directly, without requiring an additional type-filter click. Each repository result has a link whose accessible name is exactly its repository name, while the result also displays its owner/name metadata. Clicking it opens a heading containing the repository name; reloading preserves that overview. A query with no matching repository displays “No results”, including when the visitor returns home and repeats the same query. Seed data provides a named public repository and a private repository inaccessible to visitors; searching the private name exposes no result link for it. Visitors or signed-in users can search repositories they are authorized to view. The system accepts a search query, applies repository-oriented filters or scope constraints, and displays matching repositories with sufficient metadata for the user to open the target repository.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-repository-search-results.png)

requirement_quotes.REQ-1-1-2:
This feature builds on the persisted objects. The sign-in page is the form on the account-access page containing “Username or email”, “Password”, and “Sign in”. A “session” is the current-browser login record saved after successful account authentication, represented in the frontend by the upper-right account menu and access to protected pages. The visitor enters a username or email and a password and submits the form. The system looks up the account and validates its credentials and availability status; if authentication fails due to an unknown username/email, incorrect password, or unavailable account, the system displays exactly the same generic failure message “Invalid credentials”, does not disclose whether the account exists or which credential was wrong, and does not create a session. After successful authentication, the system stores a session with a unique session identifier, account identifier, and active status, then redirects to the workspace accessible to that user; the session remains valid after refreshing or reopening the workspace, and subsequent protected organization, repository, and work-item requests must use this session to determine the current user.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-sign-in.png)

cases.title: REQ-3-2-1: default personal namespace creates initialized Private repository and saved README
cases.basis: Atomic description + inherited role, scope, state and entry contracts; source review only
cases.requirement_quote:
This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes. The signed-in workspace provides a “New repository” link. The form labels are “Owner”, “Repository name”, and “Description”; the signed-in user's personal namespace is selected by default, so it is possible to submit without changing the owner. Visibility choices are radio controls “Public” and “Private”; initialization is a checkbox “Add a README file”; submission uses the button “Create repository”. Other defaults must allow duplicate-name and empty-name validation without further input. A successful initialized private repository shows a heading containing the new name, a visible Private marker, and a README file link; the overview persists after reload. The optional description “Repository created by Playwright” is saved when entered. An existing repository in this same default personal namespace is supplied for duplicate validation, which stays on the form and does not open the existing repository heading. On the repository-creation page, a signed-in user selects a personal or organization owner, enters a repository name and description, selects public or private visibility, and chooses whether to create an initial commit with a README. The system verifies that the user may create a repository in that owner's namespace, that the name is unique, and that the options are valid; on success, it stores the repository identifier, owner, visibility, default branch, and creator. If initialization is selected, it must also atomically create the initial branch, README file, and initial commit; failure at any step must leave no partially created repository. On success, the new repository overview page is opened.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-create-repository.png)

cases.title: REQ-3-2-2: fork records source relationship and independent readable history
cases.basis: Atomic description + inherited role, scope, state and entry contracts; source review only
cases.requirement_quote:
The source overview has a button “Fork”. The fork form contains a field labeled “Repository name” and button “Create fork”; it defaults to the signed-in user's personal namespace and an allowed visibility, permitting submission after editing only the name. Seed data supplies a readable source, a user allowed to create personal repositories, and an existing fork name in that namespace for the conflict case. Success opens a heading containing the new fork name and visible text “Forked from <source repository name>” with a source link; the heading and source relationship survive reload. On the source repository page, the user clicks “Fork”, selects a target personal or organization namespace, enters an optional new name and visibility, and clicks “Create fork”. The system creates an independent fork, copies the accessible default-branch history, records the source-repository link, and then opens the new fork overview page. This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-3-3 (View a Public Repository Overview) and REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes. A signed-in user can fork only when they have Read or higher permission on the source repository and permission to create repositories in the target personal or organization namespace; when the source repository is private, the fork must remain Private, while a public source repository may be forked as Public or Private. The system validates permissions on both ends and stores the new fork's owner, visibility, source-repository identifier, default branch, and copied accessible history; if any check fails, no fork is created.

The fork conflict seed uses the existing name `acme-docs-fork` in the target
personal namespace.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-fork-repository.png)

cases.requirement_quote:

Opening branch history directly displays these values without requiring file editing or other write actions.

cases.title: REQ-4-2-3: repository code result opens matching file with persisted code context
cases.basis: Atomic description + inherited role, scope, state and entry contracts; source review only
cases.requirement_quote:
This feature builds on the repository browsing context provided by REQ-4-1 (Browse Repository Files and Directories). A visitor can search readable file content within public repository `acme-docs` using the repository Search box, press Enter, and select the “Code” results view. Search is read-only and remains scoped to the current repository; it does not create commits or modify files. The results view provides matching file entries and opens a selected file in its repository context. Seed data provides query `search flow`, matching file `README.md` with that text visible, and absent query `no-such-token`. A matching file displays the query text and retains its file link after reload. An absent query displays a no-code-results state and retains the exact query in Search; repeating that search from the repository produces the same empty state.

cases.title: REQ-4-3-1: branch live selector switches file snapshot and persists current page branch
cases.basis: Atomic description + inherited role, scope, state and entry contracts; source review only
cases.requirement_quote:
This feature builds on the repository Code page provided by REQ-4-1 (Browse Repository Files and Directories). Any user with repository-view permission can use the branch selector to list and switch the branches available to the current repository. The current branch is reflected consistently by the selector, page entry, and file list; selecting a branch changes the browsing snapshot without creating a commit or rewriting branch history. The selector is a unique button named “Branch <current branch name>”; it opens a textbox named “Find branch” and selectable options whose exact accessible names are branch names. As the user types, matching options or a “No matching branch” state update without requiring Enter or a separate search action. Seed data provides public repository `branch-switch-demo`, active branch `main`, target branch `feature-search`, target-only file `main-only.md`, and unknown query `missing-branch`. Selecting `feature-search` immediately updates the selector and exposes the target-only file. Escape closes the selector; an unmatched query leaves the active branch unchanged, including after reload.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-branch-selector.png)

cases.title: REQ-4-4: file creation persists exact contents
cases.basis: Atomic description + inherited role, scope, state and entry contracts; source review only
cases.requirement_quote:
This feature builds on repository browsing and sign-in provided by REQ-4-1 (Browse Repository Files and Directories) and REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account). From a writable Code page, a contributor can use “Add file” → “Create new file” to add a file on the current branch. Only Write, Maintain, Admin, or organization Owner may submit file changes; Read and Triage may browse but may not write. A successful submission creates one commit containing the path, content, commit message, author, parent commit, and target branch, then advances that branch head. The editor exposes a “File name” field, a “File contents” textbox, a “Commit message” field, and a “Commit changes” button. New file paths cannot be empty, start with `/`, contain a `..` path segment, or conflict with an existing file or directory. Commit messages must contain 1–72 non-empty characters after trimming whitespace. Invalid submissions must leave file data, branch head, and commit history unchanged; an invalid path is reported as “Invalid file path”, while a missing message is reported as “Commit message is required”. Seed data provides public repository `file-management-demo` and Write contributor `file-contributor`. A valid unique file such as `pw-file-<unique suffix>.md`, nonempty content, and message `Add <file name>` produce a file view containing the saved content; the file's “Commits” link exposes the submitted message.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-web-file-editor.png)

From a writable Code page, a contributor can use “Add file” → “Create new file” to add a file on the current branch. Only Write, Maintain, Admin, or organization Owner may submit file changes; Read and Triage may browse but may not write. A successful submission creates one commit containing the path, content, commit message, author, parent commit, and target branch, then advances that branch head. The editor exposes a “File name” field, a “File contents” textbox, a “Commit message” field, and a “Commit changes” button. New file paths cannot be empty, start with `/`, contain a `..` path segment, or conflict with an existing file or directory. Commit messages must contain 1–72 non-empty characters after trimming whitespace. Invalid submissions must leave file data, branch head, and commit history unchanged; an invalid path is reported as “Invalid file path”, while a missing message is reported as “Commit message is required”. Seed data provides public repository `file-management-demo` and Write contributor `file-contributor`. A valid unique file such as `pw-file-<unique suffix>.md`, nonempty content, and message `Add <file name>` produce a file view containing the saved content; the file's “Commits” link exposes the submitted message.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-web-file-editor.png)

requirement_quotes.REQ-4-2-1:
This feature builds on the repository and file browsing context provided by REQ-4-1 (Browse Repository Files and Directories). A user with repository-view permission can open the repository's commit history from its repository page and inspect the records for the readable branch. Each record represents an immutable change and may expose its commit identifier, author, time, parent, and changed files. The repository page exposes a history link named “Commits”; a commit count may accompany the label without creating another matching link. Seed history includes the message `Document search flow`, author `alice-dev`, and a relative timestamp containing “ago”. Opening branch history directly displays these values without requiring file editing or other write actions.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-commit-history.png)

requirement_quotes.REQ-1-1-2:
This feature builds on the persisted objects. The sign-in page is the form on the account-access page containing “Username or email”, “Password”, and “Sign in”. A “session” is the current-browser login record saved after successful account authentication, represented in the frontend by the upper-right account menu and access to protected pages. The visitor enters a username or email and a password and submits the form. The system looks up the account and validates its credentials and availability status; if authentication fails due to an unknown username/email, incorrect password, or unavailable account, the system displays exactly the same generic failure message “Invalid credentials”, does not disclose whether the account exists or which credential was wrong, and does not create a session. After successful authentication, the system stores a session with a unique session identifier, account identifier, and active status, then redirects to the workspace accessible to that user; the session remains valid after refreshing or reopening the workspace, and subsequent protected organization, repository, and work-item requests must use this session to determine the current user.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-sign-in.png)
requirement_quotes.REQ-1-2:
This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes. The page contains exactly one button named “Account menu”; its menu contains exactly one link named “Sign out”. Activating it displays a dialog named “Sign out” with buttons named “Confirm sign out” and “Cancel”. The dialog explains that sign-out affects only the current browser session. Only “Confirm sign out” invalidates the session, while “Cancel” or closing the dialog retains the current session and page. After confirming, refresh, browser back navigation, or directly reopening a previously accessible protected account, repository, or organization page restores an unauthenticated state and displays the “Sign in” link.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-account-menu-sign-out.png)
requirement_quotes.REQ-2-2-2: An organization Owner can open a team in the organization’s “Teams” page. The team page exposes “Members” and “Settings”. On Members, “Add member” opens a visibly labeled “Username” textbox and an “Add member” button; after a valid organization member is added, the member appears in the list with a “Remove <username>” button. Removing the member updates the list immediately and remains effective after reload. On Settings, “Parent team” is a combobox and “Save” persists a parent-team change. A change that would make a team its own ancestor is rejected with “Cyclic team hierarchy is not allowed”, and the previously saved parent remains selected after reload.
requirement_quotes.REQ-2-3: A repository Admin can open “Settings” and “Manage access”. “Add people or teams” opens a picker with a visibly labeled “Search” textbox, selectable team options, a “Role” combobox, and an “Add” button. Adding a team with Write access displays the exact team name and Write role, and the grant remains visible after reload. An existing access row exposes a “Role” combobox and “Save” button; changing its role from Write to Read updates the existing record rather than creating a duplicate, and exactly one Read row remains after reload.
requirement_quotes.REQ-3-4:

cases.requirement_quote:
This feature builds on the public repository overview provided by REQ-3-3 (View a Public Repository Overview). Users with repository-view permission can read issue rows for the current repository on the Issues list page. “Open” and “Closed” are links that select status views, and the unique searchbox named “Search issues” filters matching rows as the user types without requiring Enter or a separate search button. Each result title is a link whose exact accessible name is the title. Filtering is read-only and does not modify issue data. Seed data provides public repository `acme-docs`, an Open issue titled `Improve onboarding`, and a Closed issue titled `Legacy welcome text`. The Open filter plus the known open title continues to show the matching issue after reload; the Closed filter plus the known closed title shows the closed issue and excludes the open issue.

requirement_quotes.REQ-1-1-2:
This feature builds on the persisted objects. The sign-in page is the form on the account-access page containing “Username or email”, “Password”, and “Sign in”. A “session” is the current-browser login record saved after successful account authentication, represented in the frontend by the upper-right account menu and access to protected pages. The visitor enters a username or email and a password and submits the form. The system looks up the account and validates its credentials and availability status; if authentication fails due to an unknown username/email, incorrect password, or unavailable account, the system displays exactly the same generic failure message “Invalid credentials”, does not disclose whether the account exists or which credential was wrong, and does not create a session. After successful authentication, the system stores a session with a unique session identifier, account identifier, and active status, then redirects to the workspace accessible to that user; the session remains valid after refreshing or reopening the workspace, and subsequent protected organization, repository, and work-item requests must use this session to determine the current user.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-sign-in.png)
requirement_quotes.REQ-5-1-1:
This feature builds on the public repository overview provided by REQ-3-3 (View a Public Repository Overview). Users with repository-view permission can read issue rows for the current repository on the Issues list page. “Open” and “Closed” are links that select status views, and the unique searchbox named “Search issues” filters matching rows as the user types without requiring Enter or a separate search button. Each result title is a link whose exact accessible name is the title. Filtering is read-only and does not modify issue data. Seed data provides public repository `acme-docs`, an Open issue titled `Improve onboarding`, and a Closed issue titled `Legacy welcome text`. The Open filter plus the known open title continues to show the matching issue after reload; the Closed filter plus the known closed title shows the closed issue and excludes the open issue.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-issues-list.png)
requirement_quotes.REQ-5-1-2:
The issue detail page is the read view for one uniquely numbered work item within a repository. Its heading exposes the complete issue title without the issue number, and the page displays the current Open or Closed status, the complete saved description, and discussion or activity content. Repository-view permission is sufficient to read this saved data; editable controls are available only to roles authorized for the corresponding operation. The seeded public repository `acme-docs` contains the Open issue `Improve onboarding` with description `Describe the onboarding improvement.` and discussion or activity text. Opening the issue from a visible issue entry, reloading its detail page, or reopening it from the application home page preserves the same title, description, and status.

requirement_quotes.REQ-1-1-2:
This feature builds on the persisted objects. The sign-in page is the form on the account-access page containing “Username or email”, “Password”, and “Sign in”. A “session” is the current-browser login record saved after successful account authentication, represented in the frontend by the upper-right account menu and access to protected pages. The visitor enters a username or email and a password and submits the form. The system looks up the account and validates its credentials and availability status; if authentication fails due to an unknown username/email, incorrect password, or unavailable account, the system displays exactly the same generic failure message “Invalid credentials”, does not disclose whether the account exists or which credential was wrong, and does not create a session. After successful authentication, the system stores a session with a unique session identifier, account identifier, and active status, then redirects to the workspace accessible to that user; the session remains valid after refreshing or reopening the workspace, and subsequent protected organization, repository, and work-item requests must use this session to determine the current user.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-sign-in.png)

cases.title: REQ-6-5: Maintain merge commits actual changes to base branch and persists terminal status
cases.basis: Atomic description + inherited role, scope, state and entry contracts; source review only
cases.requirement_quote: On an eligible PR, Merge pull request and then Confirm merge are buttons; confirming displays Merged, and that state remains after reload. A blocked PR keeps a visible disabled Merge pull request button and explains its unmet review or protection condition before any click. Seed data supplies a Maintain account and separate Open PRs for success and refusal. The eligible PR targets protected main, has a current non-author approval and test: success, and has no conflicts. The blocked PR targets a protected branch and lacks the required valid approval; its disabled button is accompanied by Review required by branch protection. The success and refusal states are separate PR records, so neither test relies on restoring a mutation from the other. “Merge” is the only write operation that writes the current compare commit's changes from an Open PR into the base branch; it is not simply marking the PR as complete. Only Maintain, Admin, or organization Owner may merge from the PR detail page using the sole supported “Create a merge commit” method; the merge confirmation area should display satisfied and unsatisfied conditions. Before confirmation, the system rereads the target branch head, current compare commit, merge-conflict state, and protection rules — there must be no valid Request changes; if the target is protected, each enabled rule requirement is enforced independently, requiring 1 valid non-author Approve for the current compare commit when Require 1 approval is enabled and requiring `test` success when Require status check test is enabled. An unprotected target has no additional approval-count or check-success requirement, but merging still requires no merge conflicts and no valid Request changes review. After validation succeeds, the system atomically creates a merge commit whose parents are the target-branch head at merge time and the current compare commit, updates the target-branch head, sets the PR to Merged, and stores the merger, time, and resulting commit identifier. If any condition is unsatisfied or persistence fails, the page explains the applicable reason and neither the target branch nor PR changes; a missing required approval displays “Review required by branch protection”. Merged is terminal. This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-6-3-4 (Submit a Pull Request Review) and REQ-6-1 (Protect Branches with Review and Status-Check Requirements); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

requirement_quotes.REQ-4-1:
This feature builds on the public repository overview provided by REQ-3-3 (View a Public Repository Overview). A visitor with repository-view permission can use the Code page to browse the selected branch's directory hierarchy and open files without changing repository data. Directory and file entries are links with their exact accessible names; a directory identifies the current path and a file page displays the stored file name, path, branch context, and readable content. Seed data provides public repository `acme-docs`, directory `src`, text file `README.md`, and expected content `Document search flow`. Opening the directory and then the file displays that content, and reloading the file page preserves the same read-only content.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-code-file-browser.png)

requirement_quotes.REQ-1-1-2:
This feature builds on the persisted objects. The sign-in page is the form on the account-access page containing “Username or email”, “Password”, and “Sign in”. A “session” is the current-browser login record saved after successful account authentication, represented in the frontend by the upper-right account menu and access to protected pages. The visitor enters a username or email and a password and submits the form. The system looks up the account and validates its credentials and availability status; if authentication fails due to an unknown username/email, incorrect password, or unavailable account, the system displays exactly the same generic failure message “Invalid credentials”, does not disclose whether the account exists or which credential was wrong, and does not create a session. After successful authentication, the system stores a session with a unique session identifier, account identifier, and active status, then redirects to the workspace accessible to that user; the session remains valid after refreshing or reopening the workspace, and subsequent protected organization, repository, and work-item requests must use this session to determine the current user.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-sign-in.png)
requirement_quotes.REQ-4-2-1:
This feature builds on the repository and file browsing context provided by REQ-4-1 (Browse Repository Files and Directories). A user with repository-view permission can open the repository's commit history from its repository page and inspect the records for the readable branch. Each record represents an immutable change and may expose its commit identifier, author, time, parent, and changed files. The repository page exposes a history link named “Commits”; a commit count may accompany the label without creating another matching link. Seed history includes the message `Document search flow`, author `alice-dev`, and a relative timestamp containing “ago”. Opening branch history directly displays these values without requiring file editing or other write actions.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-commit-history.png)
requirement_quotes.REQ-4-2-2:
This feature builds on the read-only history context provided by REQ-4-2-1 (View Repository Commit History). A user with repository-view permission can inspect the difference represented by a readable commit and its parent revision. The comparison is read-only: it displays changed files and numeric additions and deletions without creating a review, comment, commit, or branch change. Seed data provides an accessible commit entry in public repository `acme-docs` and changed file `src/search.ts`; opening that entry displays the changed-file path, a “Changed files” summary, and numeric additions and deletions.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-commit-diff.png)
requirement_quotes.REQ-4-4:
This feature builds on repository browsing and sign-in provided by REQ-4-1 (Browse Repository Files and Directories) and REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account). From a writable Code page, a contributor can use “Add file” → “Create new file” to add a file on the current branch. Only Write, Maintain, Admin, or organization Owner may submit file changes; Read and Triage may browse but may not write. A successful submission creates one commit containing the path, content, commit message, author, parent commit, and target branch, then advances that branch head. The editor exposes a “File name” field, a “File contents” textbox, a “Commit message” field, and a “Commit changes” button. New file paths cannot be empty, start with `/`, contain a `..` path segment, or conflict with an existing file or directory. Commit messages must contain 1–72 non-empty characters after trimming whitespace. Invalid submissions must leave file data, branch head, and commit history unchanged; an invalid path is reported as “Invalid file path”, while a missing message is reported as “Commit message is required”. Seed data provides public repository `file-management-demo` and Write contributor `file-contributor`. A valid unique file such as `pw-file-<unique suffix>.md`, nonempty content, and message `Add <file name>` produce a file view containing the saved content; the file's “Commits” link exposes the submitted message.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-web-file-editor.png)
requirement_quotes.REQ-6-1:
A branch protection rule is persistent data bound to an exact branch.
A repository Admin can open Settings and Branches, create a rule with `Branch
name pattern`, `Require 1 approval`, and `Require status check test`, and see it
after reload. Non-Admins cannot create the rule. On an Open PR, an Admin can set
the `test` check from pending to success; the saved status and setter remain after
reload. Each scenario has independent accounts and seed state.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-branch-protection.png)
requirement_quotes.REQ-6-3-3:
A non-author reviewer with permission to review can use an `Add comment`
button on a changed line in Files changed. The resulting editor is labeled
`Comment`; `Add single comment` publishes it immediately, while `Start a review`
saves it as a pending review comment. The exact entered body remains visible
after reload in both applicable states.
requirement_quotes.REQ-6-3-4:
From Files changed, a non-author reviewer can use `Review changes`
to open a form with Approve and Request changes radio controls, an optional
summary/comment field, and `Submit review`. Approve creates visible Approved
status. Request changes stores and displays the exact summary with Changes
requested status, which persists after reload.

cases.basis: Atomic description + inherited role, scope, state and entry contracts; source review only
cases.requirement_quote: The PR page provides Close pull request and Reopen pull request as buttons for authorized users. Close pull request immediately sets Closed without an extra confirmation dialog, then Reopen pull request immediately restores Open. After reload, Close pull request is available again. For a viewer who is neither author nor Maintain/Admin/Owner, both controls are absent, rather than merely disabled or rejected after activation. Seed data supplies the author and a separate Read viewer, an authored Open PR for the close/reopen cycle, and a separate Open PR readable by that viewer for permission validation. When the proposed change should not proceed, the PR author, Maintain, Admin, or organization Owner may close an unmerged Open or Draft PR without merging; the same roles may reopen a Closed PR as Open. The system stores the status, operator, and time and records the transition, while keeping the PR discussion, reviews, diff, and branch references viewable; closing or reopening must not update any branch. Merged is terminal, the page does not display close or reopen operations, and the server rejects status changes. This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-6-2-3 (Create a Pull Request from Comparison Results) and REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

requirement_quotes.REQ-6-5: On an eligible PR, Merge pull request and then Confirm merge are buttons; confirming displays Merged, and that state remains after reload. A blocked PR keeps a visible disabled Merge pull request button and explains its unmet review or protection condition before any click. Seed data supplies a Maintain account and separate Open PRs for success and refusal. The eligible PR targets protected main, has a current non-author approval and test: success, and has no conflicts. The blocked PR targets a protected branch and lacks the required valid approval; its disabled button is accompanied by Review required by branch protection. The success and refusal states are separate PR records, so neither test relies on restoring a mutation from the other. “Merge” is the only write operation that writes the current compare commit's changes from an Open PR into the base branch; it is not simply marking the PR as complete. Only Maintain, Admin, or organization Owner may merge from the PR detail page using the sole supported “Create a merge commit” method; the merge confirmation area should display satisfied and unsatisfied conditions. Before confirmation, the system rereads the target branch head, current compare commit, merge-conflict state, and protection rules — there must be no valid Request changes; if the target is protected, each enabled rule requirement is enforced independently, requiring 1 valid non-author Approve for the current compare commit when Require 1 approval is enabled and requiring `test` success when Require status check test is enabled. An unprotected target has no additional approval-count or check-success requirement, but merging still requires no merge conflicts and no valid Request changes review. After validation succeeds, the system atomically creates a merge commit whose parents are the target-branch head at merge time and the current compare commit, updates the target-branch head, sets the PR to Merged, and stores the merger, time, and resulting commit identifier. If any condition is unsatisfied or persistence fails, the page explains the applicable reason and neither the target branch nor PR changes; a missing required approval displays “Review required by branch protection”. Merged is terminal. This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-6-3-4 (Submit a Pull Request Review) and REQ-6-1 (Protect Branches with Review and Status-Check Requirements); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

requirement_quotes.REQ-1-1-2:
This feature builds on the persisted objects. The sign-in page is the form on the account-access page containing “Username or email”, “Password”, and “Sign in”. A “session” is the current-browser login record saved after successful account authentication, represented in the frontend by the upper-right account menu and access to protected pages. The visitor enters a username or email and a password and submits the form. The system looks up the account and validates its credentials and availability status; if authentication fails due to an unknown username/email, incorrect password, or unavailable account, the system displays exactly the same generic failure message “Invalid credentials”, does not disclose whether the account exists or which credential was wrong, and does not create a session. After successful authentication, the system stores a session with a unique session identifier, account identifier, and active status, then redirects to the workspace accessible to that user; the session remains valid after refreshing or reopening the workspace, and subsequent protected organization, repository, and work-item requests must use this session to determine the current user.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-sign-in.png)
requirement_quotes.REQ-4-2-1:
This feature builds on the repository and file browsing context provided by REQ-4-1 (Browse Repository Files and Directories). A user with repository-view permission can open the repository's commit history from its repository page and inspect the records for the readable branch. Each record represents an immutable change and may expose its commit identifier, author, time, parent, and changed files. The repository page exposes a history link named “Commits”; a commit count may accompany the label without creating another matching link. Seed history includes the message `Document search flow`, author `alice-dev`, and a relative timestamp containing “ago”. Opening branch history directly displays these values without requiring file editing or other write actions.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-commit-history.png)
requirement_quotes.REQ-4-2-2:
This feature builds on the read-only history context provided by REQ-4-2-1 (View Repository Commit History). A user with repository-view permission can inspect the difference represented by a readable commit and its parent revision. The comparison is read-only: it displays changed files and numeric additions and deletions without creating a review, comment, commit, or branch change. Seed data provides an accessible commit entry in public repository `acme-docs` and changed file `src/search.ts`; opening that entry displays the changed-file path, a “Changed files” summary, and numeric additions and deletions.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-commit-diff.png)
requirement_quotes.REQ-4-4:
This feature builds on repository browsing and sign-in provided by REQ-4-1 (Browse Repository Files and Directories) and REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account). From a writable Code page, a contributor can use “Add file” → “Create new file” to add a file on the current branch. Only Write, Maintain, Admin, or organization Owner may submit file changes; Read and Triage may browse but may not write. A successful submission creates one commit containing the path, content, commit message, author, parent commit, and target branch, then advances that branch head. The editor exposes a “File name” field, a “File contents” textbox, a “Commit message” field, and a “Commit changes” button. New file paths cannot be empty, start with `/`, contain a `..` path segment, or conflict with an existing file or directory. Commit messages must contain 1–72 non-empty characters after trimming whitespace. Invalid submissions must leave file data, branch head, and commit history unchanged; an invalid path is reported as “Invalid file path”, while a missing message is reported as “Commit message is required”. Seed data provides public repository `file-management-demo` and Write contributor `file-contributor`. A valid unique file such as `pw-file-<unique suffix>.md`, nonempty content, and message `Add <file name>` produce a file view containing the saved content; the file's “Commits” link exposes the submitted message.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-web-file-editor.png)
requirement_quotes.REQ-6-1:
A branch protection rule is persistent data bound to an exact branch.
A repository Admin can open Settings and Branches, create a rule with `Branch
name pattern`, `Require 1 approval`, and `Require status check test`, and see it
after reload. Non-Admins cannot create the rule. On an Open PR, an Admin can set
the `test` check from pending to success; the saved status and setter remain after
reload. Each scenario has independent accounts and seed state.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-branch-protection.png)
requirement_quotes.REQ-6-3-3:
A non-author reviewer with permission to review can use an `Add comment`
button on a changed line in Files changed. The resulting editor is labeled
`Comment`; `Add single comment` publishes it immediately, while `Start a review`
saves it as a pending review comment. The exact entered body remains visible
after reload in both applicable states.
requirement_quotes.REQ-6-3-4:
From Files changed, a non-author reviewer can use `Review changes`
to open a form with Approve and Request changes radio controls, an optional
summary/comment field, and `Submit review`. Approve creates visible Approved
status. Request changes stores and displays the exact summary with Changes
requested status, which persists after reload.

requirement_quotes.REQ-2-2-2: An organization Owner can open a team in the organization’s “Teams” page. The team page exposes “Members” and “Settings”. Removing the member updates the list immediately and remains effective after reload. On Settings, “Parent team” is a combobox and “Save” persists a parent-team change. A change that would make a team its own ancestor is rejected with “Cyclic team hierarchy is not allowed”, and the previously saved parent remains selected after reload.
